newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers push bill to deregulate U.S. sugar market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers push bill to deregulate U.S. sugar market.

text.p: One year after the House narrowly voted to retain the U.S. sugar subsidies, two lawmakers are launching a new attack on the price support program.

Representatives Dan Miller and Charles Schumer called a news conference for Thursday at 1130 EDT/1630 GMT to unveil their bill. Like last year, their plan calls for lowering the sugar loan rate and for a larger volume of imports to reduce the average U.S. market price.
Several consumer, taxpayer and food industry groups were expected to support the bill.
Sugar-grower groups have spent the past several weeks trying to outflank Miller, R-Fla., and Schumer, D-N.Y.
They have brought farmers to Washington and held a series of meetings on Capitol Hill to tell members of Congress that the sugar program means stable prices and a reliable supply for consumers.
As a result, the outlook is "much more favorable" if a vote is called on the Miller-Schumer bill, said Luther Markwart of the American Sugarbeet Growers Association.
"You find a lot of members saying this Congress has to stand by the commitments it made," he said, referring to the seven-year "Freedom to Farm" policy law passed last year.

The 1996 farm law effectively reduced the sugar support price by one cent, to 17 cents per lb, increased a deficit-reduction assessment collected on sugar marketings and eliminated domestic marketing allotments.
"We've already been reformed," said Jack Roney, economics director of the American Sugar Alliance, a grower group.
Critics like Miller, Schumer and the consumer group Public Voice for Food and Health Policy say the sugar program costs consumers more than $1 billion a year in higher food costs.
Under the program, the loan rate effectively sets the minimum price for sugar. A tariff-rate quota constrains imports and prevents domestic prices from falling below the loan rate.

The Miller-Schumer plan would lower the loan rate to 14 cents per lb over five years, set the loan rate as the maximum market price and demand farmers repay the loan. At present, farmers can forfeit the sugar instead of repaying the loan if market prices are low and imports are less than 1.5 million short tons per year.

It was assumed within the sugar industry that the Miller-Schumer bill had little future as a separate piece of legislation. The authors were expected to try to attach parts of it to the fiscal 1998 agriculture appropriations bill. Miller is a member of the Appropriations Committee.
